items.a: It depends on team size more than sticker price. Webflow's cheapest plan with a custom domain, Basic, costs $25 a month but has no CMS; a blog needs Premium at $39 a month instead. Framer's cheapest plan, Basic, costs $15 a month and already includes a small CMS, 2 collections and 1,000 items, though that price is only Basic's lowest AI-credit tier and rises if a heavier tier is picked. The gap grows with people and traffic. A solo site costs $39 a month on Webflow against $15 on Framer. An eight-editor team pushes Webflow to $732 a month, mostly from a bandwidth add-on, while the same team on Framer runs $255 a month, though that number likely understates Framer's real bandwidth cost, since Framer publishes no way to estimate it at that traffic level.

items.q: Which is easier to use, Webflow or Framer?
items.a: Framer, for most people who don't already know how to code. Its plans lean on AI design and content agents that can draft a page or copy from a prompt, and the workspace's first editor is free on every plan, so a solo owner can start without paying for help. Webflow works the other way: its own pricing page isn't built for owners who want a simple template editor with no design learning curve, because its visual canvas gives near-code-level control over layout, plus custom code on Basic and Premium and code components on Premium. That control is exactly why designers and technically comfortable teams tend to prefer Webflow: it takes longer to learn, but nothing about the layout is off-limits once you do.

items.q: Can I sell products directly through Webflow or Framer?
items.a: Only Webflow, and only up to a point. Its Ecommerce plans run from Ecommerce Standard at $42 a month, which adds a 2% transaction fee on top of whatever Stripe or PayPal already charges, up through Ecommerce Advanced, which drops that fee to 0% and raises the catalog cap to 15,000 items. Framer has no cart or checkout system on any plan, Basic, Pro or Enterprise, so a site built there can only sell something by linking out to a separate checkout tool or embedding one. Neither platform is a real fit for a business built around a physical product catalog: Webflow's own Ecommerce tiers cap out well below what a growing store needs, and a dedicated platform built for inventory, shipping and checkout is worth the switch once sales become the main point of the site.

items.q: Why does Framer's price sometimes look different from the $15 or $45 advertised?
items.a: Because that headline price is only Framer's lowest AI-credit tier, and the same plan card lets you pick a higher one. Basic's $15-a-month price assumes 1,000 AI credits a month; picking 15,000 credits from the same dropdown raises Basic itself to $225 a month. Pro works the same way: its $45-a-month price assumes 3,000 credits, and the top tier, 100,000 credits, raises Pro to $1,500 a month. Billed annually the same top tiers cost less, $150 and $1,000 respectively, but the mechanism is identical: the plan's own sticker price moves with a dropdown selection, not a separate add-on charged on top of it. Anyone comparing this price to Webflow's flat Premium plan should check which credit tier that $15 or $45 actually assumes before treating it as final.

items.q: Does adding team members cost more on Webflow or Framer?
items.a: Per seat, Framer is cheaper; in total, Webflow can go higher because it has no cap. Framer charges $30 a month for a second Full Editor or $15 a month for a content-only Content Editor seat, the same rate whether the site is on Basic or Pro, with the workspace's first editor always free. Webflow charges more per seat, $45 a month for a Full seat or $19 a month for a Limited seat, but sells as many as a team needs. Framer's ceiling is the catch: Basic and Pro both cap a single workspace at 10 total editors, and only a custom Enterprise quote removes it. A team of eight fits comfortably under that cap; a growing agency running several client sites out of one workspace can hit it faster than the per-seat savings would suggest.

items.q: Can I move my site from Framer to Webflow, or the other way, later?
items.a: Plan on a rebuild either direction, and expect Framer's side to be the harder move. Webflow gives a documented, partial way out: any paid Workspace plan, not the free Starter Workspace, can export a site's HTML and CSS, and CMS content exports one Collection at a time, though forms and server-side logic stop working once you leave. Framer publishes no equivalent: its own help center runs an article titled 'Can I export my website to HTML and self-host it?', and the answer is no, because a published Framer site depends on Framer's backend rather than shipping as a static file. Billing doesn't lock you in on either side by default, since both run month to month unless you choose annual billing, but switching a Framer site from annual back to monthly isn't self-serve; it needs a support request, and unused annual value converts to non-refundable credit.

items.q: Which is better for an agency running several client sites?
items.a: Webflow, mainly because of how it handles seats and staging. Its Freelancer Workspace, $24 a month, and Agency Workspace, $42 a month, both bundle staging sites and free client seats attached to each individual site, and Webflow sells extra paid seats with no cap on top of that. Framer has no equivalent workspace tier built for multiple clients: every editor, across every site in a workspace, counts against the same 10-seat total, so an agency juggling several active client sites can hit that ceiling well before Webflow's per-seat cost catches up. Framer still fits a freelancer running a handful of small client sites cheaply, since its $15 Basic plan already includes a CMS that Webflow's matching Basic plan doesn't have, but at real agency scale, the seat cap becomes the deciding factor.
